title: Purpose clauses
deck: Saying why something is done: ut or ne, a verb in the imperfect subjunctive, and a clause that answers the question "what for?"
desc: GCSE Latin grammar: purpose clauses with ut and ne, the imperfect subjunctive, how to translate them, what not to confuse them with, and sentences to translate and mark.
key: imperfect subjunctive, usually last in its clause
the infinitive with -t or -nt on the end: servare-t

blocks.lead: A purpose clause tells you why someone does something. In English we usually say "to" or "in order to": the soldiers hurried to the city to save the citizens. Latin does it with a small clause of its own, introduced by ut and with its verb in the subjunctive.

example.la: milites ad urbem festinaverunt <u class="c">ut</u> cives <u class="v">servarent</u>.
example.en: The soldiers hurried to the city to save the citizens.
example.note: ut opens the clause, servarent (imperfect subjunctive) closes it. Everything between them belongs to the purpose.

blocks.p: The clause answers "what for?". It is never a fact: the soldiers may or may not save anyone. That is why Latin uses the subjunctive, the mood for things wished, intended or imagined rather than things that happened.

facts: ne introduces a negative purpose: "so that ... not", "in order not to". Latin never uses ut non for a purpose.
The verb of the clause is in the subjunctive and usually comes at the end of the clause.
se or suus inside the clause refers back to the subject of the main verb: servus tacuit ne dominus se puniret, "the slave kept quiet so that his master would not punish him" (the slave).

blocks.p: At GCSE the verb in a purpose clause is always in the imperfect subjunctive, because the stories you translate are told in the past. It is easy to form and easy to spot: take the present infinitive and add the personal endings.

blocks.note: Spotting it: if the verb looks like an infinitive with an ending stuck on (servare-t, fugere-nt, esse-t), it is the imperfect subjunctive. The imperfect indicative has -ba- instead (servabat, fugiebant, erat), and that is the one it is most often mixed up with.

example.la: Romani murum aedificaverunt <u class="c">ut</u> urbem <u class="v">defenderent</u>.
example.en: The Romans built a wall to defend the city.
example.note: defenderent: infinitive defendere + -nt. The Romans are plural, so the ending is plural too.

blocks.p: English has several ways to say the same thing. Any of these earns the mark, as long as the clause reads as a purpose.

facts: to: ut cives servarent, "to save the citizens". The shortest, and usually the best.
in order to, so as to: the same, a little more formal.

so that ... might / could / would: use this when the person doing the purpose is not the subject of the main verb: nuntium misi ut tibi haec diceret, "I sent a messenger so that he might tell you this".
Negative, with ne: "so that ... would not", "in order not to", "to avoid ...ing".

example.la: servus tacuit <u class="c">ne</u> dominus se <u class="v">puniret</u>.
example.en: The slave kept quiet so that his master would not punish him.
example.note: Different people, so "so that ... would not" reads better than "in order not to". se is the slave.

example.la: nuntium misi <u class="c">ut</u> tibi haec <u class="v">diceret</u>.
example.en: I sent a messenger to tell you this.
example.note: "To tell" is fine here as well, since it is obvious who does the telling.

blocks.p: ut has three other common jobs. The subjunctive and the signposts in the main clause tell them apart.

head: Looks like
How to tell
Translate
rows:
Result clause
tam fortis erat ut hostes fugerent
A signpost in the main clause: tam, tantus, tot, adeo, ita, sic. The negative is ut non, never ne.
"so ... that": he was so brave that the enemy fled.
A verb of ordering, asking or persuading before it: impero, rogo, persuadeo, moneo, oro.
"to": the master ordered the slave to work. The same English as a purpose, so either way of reading it is safe.

ut with the indicative
ut dixi, servus fugit
No subjunctive. The verb is an ordinary indicative.
"as" or "when": as I said, the slave ran away.
No signpost, no verb of ordering, imperfect subjunctive. It answers "what for?"
"to", "in order to", "so that ... might": the slave fled to be free.

facts: Find ut or ne, then find the imperfect subjunctive that closes the clause. Translate the main clause first, then add the purpose.
"To" is a complete and correct translation of ut + subjunctive. Do not write "that" for a purpose clause: "the soldiers hurried that they save the citizens" loses the mark.
ne is not non. "ne ... puniret" is "so that he would not punish", and the "not" belongs to the clause, not to the main verb.
Check who se is. In a purpose clause it points back to the subject of the main verb.
In a comprehension question, "why did the soldiers hurry?" is almost always answered by the purpose clause. Quote the Latin from ut to the verb.

blocks.p: Two short exercises. Type your answer and it is marked against a mark scheme, phrase by phrase, so you can see which part of the sentence you have and which you have not. Nothing is saved; the grammar gym is where your progress is tracked.

exercise.title: Translate it
exercise.intro: Translate each sentence into English. Any natural wording earns the marks; the scheme is looking for the sense of each phrase.

items.la: puella in horto manebat ut matrem videret.
items.model: The girl was staying in the garden to see her mother.

part.say: You have the girl, but manebat is 'was staying' or 'stayed'.

scheme.say: to see / so that she might see

trap.say: ut with the subjunctive is a purpose here: 'to see' or 'so that she might see', not 'so that she saw'.
'When' would need the indicative. videret is imperfect subjunctive, so this is a purpose: 'to see'.

items.la: cives in muris manserunt ne hostes urbem intrarent.
items.model: The citizens stayed on the walls so that the enemy would not enter the city.

trap.say: The citizens did stay. The 'not' belongs to the ne clause, not to the main verb.

scheme.say: so that the enemy would not enter / to stop the enemy entering

trap.say: ne makes the purpose negative: 'so that the enemy would not enter'.

items.la: tam fortis erat ut hostes fugerent.
items.model: He was so brave that the enemy fled.

part.say: tam is 'so', and it is the signpost that a result clause is coming.

trap.say: This is a result clause, not a purpose: tam ... ut is 'so brave that the enemy fled'. A purpose would not have tam in the main clause.
With tam in the main clause this is a result: 'so brave that the enemy fled', a thing that happened, not a plan.

items.la: pater filium ad urbem misit ut pecuniam peteret.
items.model: The father sent his son to the city to ask for money.

scheme.say: to ask for / so that he might seek
need: ((in order |so as )?to|so that (he|his son|the son|the boy) (might|could|would|may)) (ask|seek|look|get|fetch|beg|request)

trap.say: ut + subjunctive after misit is a purpose: 'to ask for', not 'where he asked'.
There is no 'because' here: ut with the subjunctive says what for, so 'to ask for money'.

items.model: As I said, the slaves had already fled.

trap.re: (so that|in order to|in order that|to) (i )?(say|speak|tell|might say|could say)
trap.say: dixi is indicative, so this ut is not a purpose at all. With the indicative it means 'as': 'as I said'.

exercise.title: Fill in the verb
exercise.intro: Type the imperfect subjunctive of the verb in brackets. Watch the ending: singular or plural?

items.la: milites castra defendebant ut cives ___ (servo, servare).
items.why: servare + -nt: the citizens, plural, are the subject of the clause.

alts.servabant: That is the imperfect indicative (-ba-). A purpose clause needs the subjunctive: servare-nt.
alts.servent: That is a present subjunctive, which you will not need at GCSE. Purpose clauses take the imperfect: servarent.

items.la: rex nuntium misit ut pacem ___ (peto, petere).
items.why: petere + -t: the one messenger is the subject.

alts.petebat: That is the imperfect indicative (-ba-). After ut in a purpose clause the verb is subjunctive: petere-t.
alts.peterent: Right form, but the subject is one messenger, nuntium: singular peteret.
alts.petivit: That is the perfect indicative. A purpose clause needs the imperfect subjunctive: peteret.

items.la: servi tacebant ne dominus iratus ___ (sum, esse).
items.why: esse + -t: the imperfect subjunctive of sum, for the one master.

alts.erat: That is the imperfect indicative. After ne the verb must be subjunctive: esse-t.
alts.fuit: That is the perfect indicative. The clause needs the imperfect subjunctive: esset.

items.la: ad forum festinavi ut amicum ___ (video, videre).

alts.vidi: That is the perfect indicative, 'I saw'. The purpose clause needs the imperfect subjunctive: vide-re-m.
alts.videbam: That is the imperfect indicative (-ba-). The subjunctive keeps the infinitive: viderem.
alts.videret: Right form, but the subject is 'I', from festinavi: viderem.

items.la: puer ad villam cucurrit ut matrem ___ (moneo, monere).

alts.monebat: That is the imperfect indicative (-ba-), which looks similar but has no place in a purpose clause: moneret.
alts.monuit: That is the perfect indicative. The clause needs the imperfect subjunctive: moneret.
